messages.author: 97f9a19ea720b06c
messages.subject: IIF bimodality and item misfit
parts:
Hi,

I have a situation with a graded response model that I don't really understand. I have 10 items in a unidimensional model, with thousands of participants (5 point likert scale). Two items get very large alphas (i6 and 7 seen below). The idea here is actually to shorten the scale, but when I do that based on the highest alphas, the new model does not converge. If I remove the two items with high alphas, it works just fine. I get a similar situation if I run the same model using lavaan, i.e. very high loadings on those 2 items.

coef
$items
        a1    d1     d2     d3     d4
i1  0.549 1.882  0.350 -0.638 -1.982
i2  0.750 2.323  0.492 -0.679 -2.216
i3  0.686 1.766  0.361 -0.213 -1.965
i4  0.457 2.981  1.191 -0.020 -1.680
i5  1.243 3.218  1.012 -0.088 -1.366
i6  5.544 5.971 -0.018 -3.289 -7.243
i7  5.768 5.954  0.006 -3.028 -7.059
i8  0.628 3.982  1.967  0.732 -0.789
i9  0.605 1.271 -0.804 -2.064 -3.840
i10 0.731 3.187  1.429  0.507 -1.017

itemfit generates:
   item      Zh      S_X2 df.S_X2 p.S_X2
1   i1  5.9885  5877.797     124      0
2   i2  8.1585  3888.285     124      0
3   i3  7.9598  3648.097     124      0
4   i4  2.5492  7697.097     125      0
5   i5 16.5786  1264.656     121      0
6   i6 93.0786 72686.275      89      0
7   i7 98.3442 76835.686      90      0
8   i8  6.9820  4154.776     124      0
9   i9  4.3400  4409.540     122      0
10  i10 7.6877  9350.758     124      0

A corollary is that the IIF is... I suppose I shouldn't call it "bi-modal", but it has multiple peaks caused by those 2 items. So it's far from smoothly unimodal. Why does this occur?


Thanks in advance!

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: IIF bimodality and item misfit
parts:
These items are basically step-function items similar to what you would find in latent class models. They generally aren't all that great for latent trait models because all they really tell you is who is above some exact latent trait level. So removing them might make the most sense, otherwise placing prior distributions on them may also help to pull the slopes away from ∞ (they also seem to have some sparse categories according to the intercept terms, which might be part of the problem). Cheers.

Phil
